result.question:
RESEARCH TASK — querbeet R5, second pass: three gaps left open by the first run. Do NOT re-research ambiguity detection prior art (DuckDB/Power Query/LibreOffice/Frictionless) or Intl.NumberFormat.formatToParts — both are settled.

CONTEXT (fixed constraints, do not re-research): querbeet is a client-side ETL tool shipping as ONE single HTML file opened from file://, no server, NOTHING fetchable at runtime (fetch(), dynamic import(), module workers all fail from an opaque origin) — everything inlined at build time via Vite + vite-plugin-singlefile. Stack decided: Vue 3 SFCs, Arquero 8.0.3, PapaParse, Vue Flow 1.48.2 (node-graph editor, 5-30 nodes), hand-rolled virtualized table (50-row window over up to 500,000 rows, row height capped at ~32 px). German-speaking business users, German UI, data sources in any locale. Licence gate: permissive (MIT/ISC/BSD/Apache-2.0), no runtime key, no eligibility gate, verified from the LICENSE in the PUBLISHED npm package — not the GitHub repo (PrimeVue was caught relicensing while GitHub still showed MIT). Already settled and NOT to be revisited: Intl.NumberFormat.prototype.formatToParts is Baseline Widely available and yields group/decimal separators as discrete tokens with zero bundled locale data; @internationalized/number 3.6.7 (2026-05-28, Apache-2.0, 237 kB unpacked, no fetch/dynamic import in the tarball) is the ready-made fallback that actually parses.

GAP A — THE DATE AND NUMBER LIBRARY FIELD (the first run covered only the Intl path). For EACH candidate below give: current version, publish date on npm (flag as dormant if no release in 12 months), licence AS PUBLISHED ON NPM, minified+gzipped size, whether it needs SEPARATE per-locale data files (and how many bytes one locale costs), and whether the published bundle contains fetch(, import(, require of locale files or any runtime network access. Then answer the discriminator the first run could not: which of these actually PARSE a locale-formatted string back to a value, and which only FORMAT one.
Candidates: date-fns v4 + date-fns/locale (does `parse` with a locale option work, and what does importing de + en-US cost?), dayjs + customParseFormat + localeData + the de locale, luxon (its fromFormat with a locale), Temporal (is it shipping in Chromium 143+/Firefox 143+ as of mid-2026 — and does Temporal.PlainDate.from help parsing localized input at all, or only ISO?), chrono-node, any-date-parser, d3-format and d3-time-format (d3.timeParse / d3.formatLocale / d3.timeFormatLocale — these take a locale DEFINITION object rather than a tag, which is a different shape worth reporting), numbro, autonumeric, currency.js, dinero.js. Also: is there any maintained library dedicated to locale-aware number PARSING besides @internationalized/number? Report clearly which candidates are eliminated by the single-file gate versus by size versus by not parsing at all. Throughput evidence (parsing 100,000 x 20 values) if any published benchmark exists — otherwise say so plainly rather than guessing.

GAP B — TYPING THE COMPARISON VALUE IN A DECLARATIVE FILTER (the first run verified only Frictionless Table Schema, whose answer is: the physical value MAY be a JSON primitive or a castable string, but comparison MUST be against the logical parsed representation). Now check the other formats and report, per format, whether the comparison value is TYPED, COERCED, or REQUIRED TO MATCH the field type — and what documented failure modes exist when it goes wrong:
- JSONLogic (its documented loose-equality/`==` semantics and any strict variant)
- MongoDB query documents (BSON type bracketing / comparison order — does {"amount": {"$gt": "1000"}} match numeric documents at all?)
- Elasticsearch Query DSL (the `coerce` mapping parameter, range queries against numeric fields with string bounds, and what happens on mapping conflict)
- OData $filter (its ABNF literal grammar — are numeric literals unquoted by grammar?)
- GraphQL filter input types (Int/Float/String scalars, coercion rules in the spec)
- Vega-Lite filter transforms and its `datum` typing
- RQL / JSON:API filter conventions (typed vs untyped, and how implementations disambiguate)
- Sigma detection rules (its documented string-vs-number matching semantics)
Then: LLM-FACING SCHEMA PRACTICE. What does published guidance from OpenAI structured outputs, Anthropic tool-use/JSON schema docs, and any measured study say about making a numeric-versus-string JSON field unambiguous to a model — does `anyOf: [number, string]` help or hurt determinism, do `description` fields and few-shot examples measurably change what a model emits, and is there evidence that a UNION type makes model output LESS consistent? This matters because a measured spike found five independent LLM authors split four-to-one between "1000" and 1000 for the same task.

GAP C — CSS FOR A SINGLE-FILE OFFLINE APP (not researched at all in the first run). The UI is three panes: a Sources list, a Vue Flow node-graph canvas with 5-30 nodes carrying per-kind configuration forms, and a dense virtualized data table. Hard constraints: NO external stylesheet, NO web font, NO icon font, NO runtime fetch of any kind — every byte inlined at build time by vite-plugin-singlefile; system font stack only; must work from file://.
Compare Pico.css v2, Tailwind CSS v4, UnoCSS, Open Props, Bulma, Water.css, Simple.css and hand-written CSS with Vue SFC `<style scoped>`. For each: current version and release date, licence on npm, and the decisive number — the INLINED CSS BYTE COST for an app of this shape (Tailwind v4 and UnoCSS emit only used utilities, so their cost is a function of the app, not of the framework; classless frameworks like Pico ship a fixed stylesheet — quantify both honestly, and say when a figure is a vendor claim rather than a measurement). Specifically check: (1) does Tailwind v4's Oxide engine or its `@import "tailwindcss"` entry require anything at RUNTIME, or is it purely build-time? (2) do any of these ship @font-face rules or url() references to external assets that would break the no-fetch gate or silently bloat the inlined file? (3) does Vue Flow's own required stylesheet (@vue-flow/core/dist/style.css and theme-default.css) conflict with a utility framework's preflight/reset — this is a documented friction point worth checking; (4) what does a CSS framework cost in AUTHORING friction for dense tables and per-node forms versus plain scoped CSS with custom properties?

OUTPUT REQUIREMENTS:
- Cited markdown. NO HTML, NO artifact.
- Every library claim states version, publish date, npm licence, min+gzip size, and runtime-fetch status. If a number is a vendor self-report, label it as such.
- Distinguish MEASURED/documented from inferred. Name anything that needs a local measurement.
- One concrete recommendation per gap, with the runner-up and why it lost.
- Primary sources: npm registry metadata, official docs, spec texts, GitHub issues with reproductions. Blog posts are weak evidence.
result.summary: Of the second-pass research, only Gap A (the date/number library field) produced claims that survived 3-vote adversarial verification; Gaps B (typing the comparison value in declarative filters) and C (CSS for a single-file offline app) produced no surviving claims and remain unresearched. On Gap A the parse-vs-format discriminator resolves cleanly: date-fns 4.4.0 (npm 2026-05-29, MIT verified in the tarball, zero runtime deps, zero fetch/XHR/dynamic-import in any shipped .js/.cjs), Luxon 3.7.2 (npm 2025-09-05, MIT) and d3-time-format all genuinely PARSE locale-formatted strings back to values, Day.js parses only after explicitly registering the separate customParseFormat plugin (dayjs.min.js 3,049 B gzip + plugin 1,863 B gzip, MIT, 1.11.21), and Temporal is eliminated twice over — Temporal.PlainDate.from() accepts only Temporal objects, property bags and RFC 9557 strings (so "31.12.2025" throws), and Temporal is not Baseline because Safari does not ship it at all (Chrome/Edge 144, Firefox 139, Node 26 — the brief's "143+/143+" premise is wrong). The decisive cross-cutting fact is that NONE of the verified candidates infers a locale from the input string: every one requires the caller to supply an explicit format pattern (or a localized L/LL token plus a named locale), so the ambiguity-detection burden stays in querbeet's own code and the library is only the executor. Recommendation for Gap A is date-fns 4.4.0 `parse` with per-locale `match`, runner-up d3-time-format for its inlinable locale-definition objects; Luxon loses on absolute throughput (356 ms per 100,000 values even with its precompiled parser, i.e. ~7 s for 100,000 x 20 single-threaded, locally measured).

findings.claim: Temporal is eliminated from Gap A on two independent grounds: it cannot parse locale-formatted dates at all, and it is not Baseline because Safari does not ship it.
findings.evidence: MDN (fetched 2026-08-01) enumerates the ONLY accepted inputs to Temporal.PlainDate.from(): a Temporal.PlainDate/PlainDateTime/ZonedDateTime instance, an RFC 9557 string, or a property bag {year, month, day, monthCode, era/eraYear, calendar}. The only options property is `overflow` ("constrain"|"reject") — there is no format-pattern or locale hook anywhere in the signature, so there is no way to feed "31.12.2025" plus a de-DE hint. The RFC 9557 grammar is YYYY-MM-DD[u-ca=calendar_id] with components separated by `-` or nothing; dot separators and DMY ordering are outside the grammar and produce a RangeError, not a reinterpretation. The TC39 proposal docs corroborate: "it must be a string, which is expected to be in RFC 9557 format, or a subset of that format that includes at least the date portion." The asymmetry is explicit in the API surface — toLocaleString() exists for localized OUTPUT, there is no inverse. Separately, both MDN Temporal pages carry verbatim: "Limited availability: This feature is not Baseline because it does not work in some of the most widely-used browsers." MDN browser-compat-data raw JSON (javascript/builtins/Temporal/PlainDate.json) gives Chrome 144, Edge 144, Firefox 139, Node 26.0.0, Safari NOT SUPPORTED, standard-track, no flags; caniuse.com/temporal agrees (Firefox 135-138 flagged off) and puts global support at 67.12%. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF'S PREMISE: the shipping versions are Chromium/Edge 144 and Firefox 139, not "143+/143+". For a single HTML file opened from file:// in whatever browser the user has, with no build-time browser targeting and no polyfill fetchable at runtime, a ~33%-of-users hard ReferenceError is disqualifying — and even where Temporal ships it delivers zero parsing benefit.

LICENCE VERIFIED FROM THE PUBLISHED TARBALL, not GitHub (the PrimeVue guard): date-fns-4.4.0.tgz, 1,594,616 B packed / 10,902,084 B unpacked / 5,136 files, sha256 eb106d1e9276213d6144b221c103e4abb7d92186734f7505f5a3860427b41a06; package/LICENSE.md is the full MIT text, "Copyright (c) 2021 Sasha Koss and Lesha Koss". The registry document carries license:"MIT". PARSES: `./parse` is a published export subpath ({"import":{"types":"./parse.d.ts","default":"./parse.js"},...}). parse.d.ts:15 — `export interface ParseOptions<DateType extends Date = Date> extends LocalizedOptions<"options"|"match"|"formatLong">, FirstWeekContainsDateOptions, WeekOptions, AdditionalTokensOptions, ContextOptions<DateType>`. parse.d.ts:299 documents `@throws options.locale must contain match property`. The parsing machinery is confirmed at RUNTIME, not just in types: parse.js:348 `const locale = options?.locale ?? defaultOptions.locale ?? defaultLocale;` and parse.js:432 passes `locale.match` into the token parser; locale/de.js:18-32 carries `match: match` alongside localize/formatLong and has both named and default exports. The shipped JSDoc example parses a non-English month name: `parse('28-a de februaro', "do 'de' MMMM", new Date(2010,0,1), { locale: eo })` => Sun Feb 28 2010.
NO RUNTIME FETCH: the grep `fetch\(|XMLHttpRequest|[^.a-zA-Z]import\(` over all *.js/*.cjs returned exactly ONE file, package/docs/config.js, whose sole match is line 1 `/** @type {import('@date-fns/docs').DateFnsDocs.Config} */` — a JSDoc type annotation in a block comment, in a file not reachable through the exports map. Extension census: 1428 .js, 1231 .cjs, 1231 .ts, 1230 .cts, 0 .mjs, so the include-globs covered every executable file. A hardened sweep (`fetch(|XMLHttpRequest|WebSocket|navigator.sendBeacon|new Worker|importScripts|require.resolve|eval(|new Function`) returned ZERO matches; `url(` in JS returned zero; all 698 files matching `https?://` match only inside JSDoc comments. Locale modules are reached by static ESM import (locale.js is a 97-line barrel of `export * from "./locale/xx.js"`; locale/de.js opens with five static imports), package.json declares `"type":"module"` and `"sideEffects":false`, so Vite/Rollup inline and tree-shake them at build time. findings.claim: Luxon 3.7.2 parses locale-formatted strings via DateTime.fromFormat with a `locale` option, and ships a documented precompiled-parser path (buildFormatParser/fromFormatParser) for bulk parsing — but even optimized it costs ~356 ms per 100,000 values.
findings.evidence:
API docs verbatim: `fromFormat(text, fmt, opts)` — "Create a DateTime from an input string and format string. Defaults to en-US if no locale has been specified, regardless of the system's locale... opts.locale (default 'en-US') — a locale string to use when parsing. Will also set the DateTime to this locale." The official parsing manual gives a non-English worked example: `DateTime.fromFormat("mai 25 1982", "LLLL dd yyyy", { locale: "fr" })`. LOCAL MEASUREMENT (luxon 3.7.2 from npm, Node): fromFormat('25. Mai 1982','d. LLLL yyyy',{locale:'de'}) -> valid, 1982-05-25; fromFormat('31.12.2024','dd.MM.yyyy',{locale:'de'}) -> 2024-12-31; CONTROL: fromFormat('Mai 25 1982','LLLL dd yyyy',{locale:'en-US'}) -> isValid false, invalidReason "unparsable". The control is decisive — the identical input flips from parsed to unparsable purely by changing `locale`, proving the option governs interpretation rather than only tagging output.
BULK PATH: docs for `buildFormatParser(fmt, options): TokenParser` — "Build a parser for fmt using the given locale. This parser can be passed to DateTime.fromFormatParser to parse a date in this format. This can be used to optimize cases where many dates need to be parsed in a specific format." Precompilation is literally true in the published tarball (npm pack luxon@3.7.2): src/impl/tokenParser.js:435 TokenParser's constructor does macro expansion, unit resolution and `RegExp(regexString,"i")` compilation up front, while explainFromTokens() — the path fromFormat takes — reconstructs a TokenParser and recompiles the RegExp on EVERY call. One-format-one-locale is ENFORCED, not advisory: datetime.js:2385 throws InvalidArgumentError when the runtime locale differs from the parser's (reproduced). MEASURED LOCALLY (not a published Luxon benchmark; no official throughput figure exists): N=100,000 strings 'dd.MM.yyyy' locale de — fromFormat 998 ms vs fromFormatParser 356 ms, 2.80x, identical results. ABSOLUTE COST IS THE PROBLEM: 356 ms per 100k means a 100,000-row x 20-date-column parse is still ~7 s single-threaded. The optimization is real; it does not by itself make Luxon fast enough.
NPM: luxon 3.7.2, published 2025-09-05T10:14:55Z, license MIT per the published package.json and LICENSE.md in the tarball, unpackedSize 4,592,735 B. ~11 months old — inside the 12-month dormancy threshold, but only just. BOUNDS: parsing is Intl-dependent ("the exact strings may in some cases be environment-specific"); ZZZZ/ZZZZZ offset-name tokens, single-letter month/weekday tokens and macro tokens containing offset names are not parseable; ambiguous zone abbreviations ("EST") are unparseable. NOT VERIFIED: Luxon's min+gzip size.

findings.claim: Day.js cannot parse a format string until the separate customParseFormat plugin is registered, and the failure mode is a SILENT WRONG RESULT rather than a throw.
findings.evidence: The docs require the two-step load verbatim: `var customParseFormat = require("dayjs/plugin/customParseFormat"); dayjs.extend(customParseFormat);`, and the string-format page states flatly "This requires the CustomParseFormat plugin to work." LOCAL REPRODUCTION (dayjs@1.11.21 from npm, Node): WITHOUT the plugin, dayjs('25.12.1995','DD.MM.YYYY').format() -> "Invalid Date" — the German shape fails outright; but dayjs('12-25-1995','MM-DD-YYYY').format() -> "1995-12-25T00:00:00+01:00", i.e. the format argument is SILENTLY IGNORED and dayjs falls through to its built-in ISO-ish/native-Date path, which happens to be right for US order and wrong for anything else. After dayjs.extend(customParseFormat), both parse correctly. That silent fallback is the correctness trap for a German-locale ETL tool and must be stated in any write-up. SIZES (measured from the installed package): dayjs.min.js 3,049 B gzip; plugin/customParseFormat.js 3,879 B raw / 1,863 B gzip — a physically separate file. Licence field in the published package.json: MIT. Latest 1.11.21, npm time.modified 2026-05-26. The published plugin source confirms the mechanism: when `format` is undefined it delegates straight back to the core parser (`i.call(this,e)`) and never runs custom parsing; there is no code path that inspects the input string to infer a date order.

findings.claim: Whether Day.js genuinely parses localized month names via a locale tag is UNRESOLVED — the strong version of that claim was refuted 0-3, while a verifier's inspection of the published source showed localized L/LL tokens do resolve against the de locale's formats. Treat Day.js locale parsing as needing a local measurement.
findings.vote: 0-3 on the strong claim; contradicted by source-level evidence in a 3-0 claim's verification notes
findings.evidence: The claim 'dayjs("2018 Enero 15","YYYY MMMM DD","es") yields 2018-01-15, therefore Day.js genuinely parses locale-formatted strings' was REFUTED 0-3 and must not be reported as verified. Pointing the other way, the verification of the (confirmed) format-string claim read the published artifacts and found that customParseFormat DOES expand localized tokens — its source contains `replace(/(\[[^\]]+])|(LTS?|l{1,4}|L{1,4})/g, ...)` resolving against `locale.formats`, with a built-in default `L: "MM/DD/YYYY"`, and the published de locale defines `formats:{LTS:"HH:mm:ss",LT:"HH:mm",L:"DD.MM.YYYY",LL:"D. MMMM YYYY",...}`. So `dayjs(s,"L","de")` should parse DD.MM.YYYY. The two lines of evidence are not formally reconciled by any surviving claim, and no confirmed claim establishes that MMMM matches German month names on the parse path. ACTION: run a local reproduction against the installed dayjs 1.11.21 for (a) dayjs('15. Januar 2018','D. MMMM YYYY','de') and (b) dayjs('15.01.2018','L','de') before relying on either behaviour.

findings.claim: d3-time-format genuinely parses via strptime-style specifiers, is STRICT (returns null on any literal mismatch), and takes locale data as a plain definition OBJECT — roughly 500 bytes of inert JSON for German — which is trivially inlinable at build time.
findings.evidence:
PARSES: docs for locale.parse — "Returns a new parser for the given string specifier. The specifier string may contain the same directives as locale.format. The %d and %e directives are considered equivalent for parsing. The returned function parses a specified string, returning the corresponding date or null if the string could not be parsed." d3.timeParse/d3.utcParse are aliases on the default locale. Confirmed in the shipped implementation (src/locale.js, newParse): returns a Date or null (`if (i != string.length) return null`), with %B->parseMonth, %b->parseShortMonth, %A->parseWeekday, %a->parseShortWeekday, %d/%e->parseDayOfMonth, and parseMonth built from locale.months via monthRe/monthLookup (`d.m = monthLookup.get(n[0].toLowerCase())`) — locale month/day NAMES are genuinely consumed on the parse path.
STRICT: docs verbatim — "Parsing is strict: if the specified string does not exactly match the associated specifier, this method returns null. For example, if the associated specifier is %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ, then the string \"2011-07-01T19:15:28Z\" will be parsed as expected, but \"2011-07-01T19:15:28\", \"2011-07-01 19:15:28\" and \"2011-07-01\" will return null" — and the docs' own remedy is the elimination argument in miniature: "If a more flexible parser is desired, try multiple formats sequentially until one returns non-null." Implementation confirms: parseSpecifier compares non-directive characters by code unit (`else if (c != string.charCodeAt(j++)) return -1;`). PRECISION FIX for the write-up: say "literal characters must match exactly (numeric fields tolerate variable digit width and leading whitespace, since numberRe = /^\s*\d+/)" rather than "character-for-character". Note the null-on-mismatch semantics is actually an ASSET for querbeet's ambiguity detection — a try-each-candidate loop gets an unambiguous reject signal.
LOCALE AS OBJECT: d3.timeFormatLocale(definition) requires exactly eight keys — dateTime (%c), date (%x), time (%X), periods, days, shortDays, months, shortMonths — and there is no BCP-47-tag entry point anywhere in the module. The published German locale, pulled from the npm tarball path on jsDelivr, is ~500 bytes of inert JSON: {"dateTime":"%A, der %e. %B %Y, %X","date":"%d.%m.%Y","time":"%H:%M:%S","periods":["AM","PM"],"days":["Sonntag",...],"shortDays":["So","Mo","Di","Mi","Do","Fr","Sa"],"months":["Januar",...],"shortMonths":["Jan","Feb","Mrz",...,"Dez"]}. No code, no loader, no side effects — a build-time import or a literal paste fully satisfies the file:// no-fetch gate. d3's docs do elsewhere demonstrate d3.json(".../locale/de-DE.json") as a convenience, but that is optional and not a requirement of timeFormatLocale. NOT VERIFIED for d3-time-format: npm version, publish date, npm licence, min+gzip size — and the parallel d3-format number-locale definition ({decimal, thousands, grouping, currency}) was not checked at all.

findings.claim: No verified candidate infers a date format from the input string — every one requires the caller to supply an explicit pattern (or a localized token plus a named locale), so ambiguity detection stays in querbeet's own code.
findings.vote: cross-cutting; supported by three unanimous claims
findings.evidence: date-fns: parse(dateStr, formatStr, referenceDate, options) — formatStr is a REQUIRED positional argument; locale.match resolves month/day names and ordinals and P/p expand via locale.formatLong (parse.d.ts:261-264, "using en-US locale: P => MM/dd/yyyy ... using pt-BR locale: P => dd/MM/yyyy"), but a bare locale tag cannot infer the pattern of an unknown string. Day.js: the format argument is mandatory — either a literal token pattern or a localized token (L/LL/LT) plus an explicitly named locale key; there is no code path that inspects the string. Luxon: fromFormat requires fmt, and buildFormatParser is bound to exactly one format+locale (enforced by a throw). d3-time-format: strict single-specifier, with the docs themselves prescribing "try multiple formats sequentially until one returns non-null". CONSEQUENCE for querbeet: the library choice does not reduce the ambiguity-detection work; the candidate-enumeration loop (try de patterns, try en-US patterns, count unambiguous vs ambiguous hits) is querbeet's own code in every case, and the library is only the per-candidate executor. This also means throughput must be budgeted as (rows x columns x candidates-tried), not (rows x columns).

findings.claim: GAP A IS ONLY PARTLY ANSWERED: seven of the thirteen named candidates produced no surviving claim, and no library-dedicated locale-aware NUMBER parser besides @internationalized/number was verified.
findings.vote: absence of claims — stated as a gap, not a finding about the libraries
findings.evidence: NOT COVERED by any surviving claim: chrono-node, any-date-parser (the two heuristic/inference parsers, and therefore the only candidates that could have contradicted the cross-cutting no-inference finding), d3-format (the NUMBER side of the d3 locale-definition pattern — {decimal, thousands, grouping, currency} — which is the direct structural analogue of the verified d3-time-format result), numbro, autonumeric, currency.js, dinero.js. findings.evidence: No claim addresses JSONLogic loose-equality/== semantics or a strict variant; MongoDB BSON type bracketing and whether {"amount":{"$gt":"1000"}} matches numeric documents; the Elasticsearch `coerce` mapping parameter, string bounds on numeric range queries, or mapping-conflict behaviour; the OData $filter ABNF literal grammar; GraphQL Int/Float/String input-coercion rules; Vega-Lite filter transforms and datum typing; RQL / JSON:API filter conventions; or Sigma detection-rule string-vs-number matching. The only settled input remains the first run's Frictionless Table Schema result (physical value MAY be a JSON primitive or a castable string; comparison MUST be against the logical parsed representation). The measured spike that motivated this gap — five independent LLM authors splitting four-to-one between "1000" and 1000 for the same task — therefore still has no external corroboration or counter-evidence. This gap needs a full re-run; do not let the absence of claims read as an absence of risk.

findings.claim: GAP C (CSS for a single-file offline app) produced ZERO surviving claims — no framework was sized, licensed, or checked against the no-fetch gate.
findings.evidence: Nothing was verified for Pico.css v2, Tailwind CSS v4, UnoCSS, Open Props, Bulma, Water.css, Simple.css, or the hand-written-scoped-CSS baseline: no current version, no release date, no npm licence, no inlined byte cost. result.caveats:
SCOPE: only Gap A produced surviving claims, and only for 6 of 13 named candidates (Temporal, date-fns, Luxon, Day.js, d3-time-format, plus the carried-over @internationalized/number). Gaps B and C produced none at all — this is a partial answer to the brief, not a complete one.

FACTUAL CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: Temporal ships in Chromium/Edge 144 and Firefox 139 (and Node 26.0.0), not "Chromium 143+/Firefox 143+". Safari does not ship it, which is why it is not Baseline; global support is 67.12% per caniuse.

MEASURED vs INFERRED. MEASURED/documented: all version, publish-date and licence facts (registry metadata plus tarball LICENSE files); date-fns's no-fetch grep (reproduced on the extracted tarball with a hardened pattern set and a full extension census); Day.js's 3,049 B / 1,863 B gzip sizes and its silent-fallback behaviour (local Node reproduction); Luxon's locale-flips-parse-result control (local Node reproduction); d3's strictness (docs plus src/locale.js). INFERRED: that Vite/Rollup will tree-shake and inline date-fns's static ESM locale imports — this is standard bundler semantics, not a measurement, and the actual inlined byte cost is unmeasured.

REFUTED — DO NOT REPORT AS FACT. Three claims failed their votes and must not leak into the write-up: (a) that date-fns's German locale costs ~6.7 kB gzip (0-3); (b) that Day.js parses "2018 Enero 15" with an "es" locale tag (0-3); (c) that Luxon's en-US parsing default constitutes a silent-wrong-result hazard requiring an explicit locale on every call (1-2) — the en-US default is documented and real, but the hazard framing did not survive.

VENDOR/SELF-REPORT LABELLING: no vendor-claimed numbers appear in this report. No PUBLISHED throughput benchmark exists for any candidate; the one throughput figure (Luxon 998 ms -> 356 ms per 100,000 dd.MM.yyyy values, 2.80x) is a verifier's single-machine Node measurement and is indicative only. The derived ~7 s for 100,000 x 20 columns is arithmetic on that measurement, single-threaded, and does not account for trying multiple format candidates per value.

MISSING NUMBERS the brief explicitly demanded: min+gzip size is unverified for date-fns, Luxon and d3-time-format; version/publish-date/npm-licence are unverified for d3-time-format. Every one of these needs a LOCAL MEASUREMENT — a Vite + vite-plugin-singlefile build importing exactly the parse path plus de and en-US, then measuring the delta in the emitted single HTML file. That build is the only honest way to compare inlined cost, and it should be run before the Gap A recommendation is committed.

TOOLING LIMITATION affecting evidence quality: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) during verification, so no verifier could sweep for third-party contradiction (GitHub issues, reproductions disputing a mechanism). Verifiers compensated by going to published tarballs and by executing code locally, which is stronger evidence for API-shape and content claims than search results would have been — but it means the "no credible contradicting source found" statements rest on primary-source agreement rather than on an adversarial search sweep.

TIME SENSITIVITY: Temporal's Baseline status turns entirely on Safari and could change; re-check before any decision that depends on it. date-fns has a 5.0.0-alpha.0 on the `next` tag (2026-05-29) and a release history of one 12-day burst after a 20-month gap — its maintenance trajectory is genuinely uncertain. Luxon's latest release is ~11 months old, close to the dormancy threshold.

MAINTENANCE-CADENCE WORDING: do not write "actively maintained" for date-fns. Write "four releases in May 2026 after a 20-month gap; packument last modified 2026-05-29."
openQuestions: Gap A recommendation, stated with its runner-up so the parent can act on it now: take date-fns 4.4.0 `parse` with per-locale `match` — it parses (verified at runtime in the shipped ESM), it is MIT verified in the tarball, it has zero runtime deps, it has zero fetch/XHR/dynamic-import in any executable file, and its locale modules are static ESM imports Vite inlines at build time. RUNNER-UP d3-time-format, which loses only on unverified metadata (no version/date/licence/size checked) — its locale-DEFINITION-OBJECT design (~500 bytes of inert JSON for de-DE) is arguably the better fit for the single-file gate, and its strict null-on-mismatch is ideal for candidate-enumeration ambiguity detection, so it should be re-examined if the date-fns local build measures badly. Luxon lost on absolute throughput (~356 ms per 100k even precompiled, ~7 s for 100k x 20) and unmeasured bundle size; Day.js lost on the silent-ignored-format-argument trap plus unresolved locale-name parsing; Temporal is eliminated outright. This recommendation is CONDITIONAL on the local Vite single-file build measuring the actual inlined delta for date-fns parse + de + en-US, since the only per-locale size figure produced was refuted 0-3.

Do chrono-node or any-date-parser actually infer a format from the string, and do they handle German dot-separated DMY? These were the only two candidates that could have contradicted the cross-cutting no-inference finding, and neither was checked. If one of them does genuine inference under a permissive licence with no runtime fetch, it changes the ambiguity-detection design materially — querbeet would delegate candidate enumeration instead of owning it.

Does d3-format mirror d3-time-format on the NUMBER side — i.e. does d3.formatLocale take a definition object ({decimal, thousands, grouping, currency}) that inlines as inert JSON, and does it PARSE or only FORMAT? The verified d3-time-format result makes this the highest-value unchecked candidate for the number half of Gap A, and it bears directly on whether @internationalized/number (237 kB unpacked) is actually needed as the fallback.

Gap B must be re-run in full, and the two halves should be sequenced: first the eight filter formats (MongoDB BSON type bracketing and Elasticsearch `coerce` are the two with the sharpest documented failure modes and should be checked against spec/manual text, not blog posts), then the LLM-facing schema question, where the operative sub-question is narrow enough to answer decisively — does published OpenAI/Anthropic structured-output guidance say anything measured about anyOf:[number,string], and does any study measure whether union types reduce output consistency? The four-to-one "1000" vs 1000 spike remains uncorroborated.

Gap C must be re-run in full, and two of its sub-questions are better settled by a local build than by search: whether Vue Flow's style.css/theme-default.css collides with a utility framework's preflight reset, and what the actual inlined CSS byte delta is for each candidate on a three-pane app of this shape. The search-answerable parts are the npm licence/version/date per framework and whether any of them ship @font-face or url() references that would break the no-fetch gate.

refuted.claim: Luxon's parsing defaults to en-US irrespective of the host system locale, so parsing German-formatted input requires explicitly passing locale: 'de' (or 'de-DE') on every fromFormat call — a silent-wrong-result hazard for a German-UI tool ingesting mixed-locale sources.

With CustomParseFormat, Day.js genuinely PARSES a locale-formatted string back to a date value — a locale tag can be passed as the third argument and localized month names are resolved, e.g. dayjs("2018 Enero 15", "YYYY MMMM DD", "es") yields 2018-01-15.

Locale data is shipped as SEPARATE per-locale modules under `./locale/*` (95 locale export subpaths in the 4.4.0 exports map, including both `./locale/de` and `./locale/en-US`), so the inlined cost scales per locale rather than being fixed. Measured on the published 4.4.0 tarball: the `locale/de.js` entry module is 985 bytes raw, and the full `locale/de/` ESM directory is 7 .js files totalling 40,366 bytes raw; entry + all seven chunks concatenated compress to 6,691 bytes gzip -9. That ~6.7 kB gzip is the pre-tree-shaking upper bound for one locale; a bundle importing only `parse`'s `match`/`formatLong` needs less, which requires a local measurement to pin down.
